title: Verifying Whole-Number Ratios from Experimental Data
notes: The computational skill behind all the combination laws: converting raw percentage/mass data into whole-number ratios — the shared method of definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions, and of empirical-formula work.

(1) Take the percentage of each element as mass in 100 g (or use the given masses). (2) Divide each mass by the atomic mass of that element → moles. (3) Divide all values by the smallest. (4) If the ratios are still fractional (e.g. 1 : 1.5, 1 : 1.33, 1 : 1.67), multiply the whole set by 2, 3 or 4 respectively to clear fractions. (5) Interpret: the whole-number ratio is the atomic ratio in the compound.

An oxide contains 60% metal and 40% oxygen (atomic mass of metal = 48). Metal = 60/48 = 1.25; O = 40/16 = 2.5. Divide by 1.25 → M : O = 1 : 2 → formula MO₂. (With 70% metal it would be 1.46 : 1.875 → 1 : 1.28… → careful: re-check data, since real ratios must resolve.)
### Worked pattern 2 — two oxides checked against multiple proportions

Oxide A: 46.7% N; oxide B: 30.4% N. Per gram of nitrogen: A has 46.7/53.3 = 0.876 g O; B has 30.4/69.6 = 0.437 g O. Ratio 0.876 : 0.437 = 2 : 1 — a whole-number ratio, so the data obey the law of multiple proportions (NO₂-type and NO-type oxides).

Real analytical data carry errors, so ratios like 1 : 1.48 may 'want' to be 1 : 1.5 while 1 : 1.35 may be measurement noise around 1 : 1.33. Judgement (and significant figures) decide; non-stoichiometric compounds (Fe₀.₉₃O) will never resolve exactly, and the method assumes the compound is a true formula compound.
confusion: ❌ Any near-integer ratio may be rounded freely. ✅ Round only with analytical justification; 1 : 1.9 is not 1 : 2 in a berthollide.
❌ The ratio is of masses. ✅ After dividing by atomic masses, the ratio is of *atoms* (moles), not grams.
❌ Multiplying changes the formula. ✅ Scaling the whole ratio set preserves it (2 : 4 is the same as 1 : 2).

universalFacts: This is exactly the arithmetic that produces empirical formulas from combustion data.

summary: This is the computational skill shared by definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions and by empirical-formula work: converting raw percentage or mass data into a whole-number atomic ratio. Take the percentage of each element as the mass in 100 g, divide each mass by the corresponding atomic mass to get moles, divide all values by the smallest, and multiply the whole set by 2, 3 or 4 if fractions remain, so that 1 : 1.5 becomes 2 : 3 and 1 : 1.33 becomes 3 : 4. The resulting whole-number ratio is the atomic ratio in the compound. Because real analytical data carry errors, judgement is needed — 1 : 1.48 may genuinely be 1 : 1.5, while 1 : 1.35 is probably noise, and non-stoichiometric compounds such as Fe₀.₉₃O will never resolve exactly.
importantConcepts: Five-step method: mass in 100 g → divide by atomic mass → divide by the smallest → clear fractions → interpret
The ratio obtained is one of atoms (moles), not of masses
Clearing fractions: ×2 for halves, ×3 for thirds, ×4 for quarters
Multipliers applied to the whole set preserve the ratio, since 2 : 4 is the same ratio as 1 : 2
Error awareness and significant figures when a ratio is only approximately integral

keyPoints: Divide by atomic masses before comparing — the ratio is of atoms, not grams.
Always state the multiplier used when clearing fractions (×2, ×3 or ×4).
Scaling the whole ratio set does not change the formula; 2 : 4 and 1 : 2 are the same ratio.
Round only with analytical justification — 1 : 1.9 is not 1 : 2 in a berthollide compound.
The whole-number ratio is the atomic ratio, which is the simplest ratio and not necessarily the molecular formula.
specialNotes: A ratio such as 1 : 1.48 may genuinely be 1 : 1.5, whereas 1 : 1.35 is probably measurement noise around 1 : 1.33 — judgement and significant figures decide.
Non-stoichiometric compounds such as Fe₀.₉₃O will never resolve to a single whole-number ratio, so the method cannot be completed for them.
The method assumes a true formula compound; for mixtures, alloys or solutions the resulting ratio has no fixed meaning.
Rounding relative atomic masses too early can shift a ratio, so carry at least one decimal place through the division.
examShortTricks: Write the whole method as five numbered steps before starting the arithmetic — the steps carry marks even if the numbers slip.
×2 for halves, ×3 for thirds, ×4 for quarters: recognise the fraction and pick the multiplier instantly.
Always show the division by the smallest value; examiners look for that line specifically.
Sanity check: the atomic ratio of a stable compound should give small whole numbers, usually not exceeding about 7 for common elements.
examNotes: Usually a 3-mark method question followed by a 2–3 mark numerical on percentage data.
The same arithmetic appears in definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions, so it is heavily reused across the unit.
Verifying multiple proportions from two percentage compositions is a common 3-mark numerical.
Answers should state the multiplier used and the interpretation of the final ratio.
